title: Even Out Coins in a Tree
statement:
You get the root of a binary tree with n nodes. Each node's value is the number of coins on it, and the tree holds exactly n coins in total.

In one move you pass a single coin from a node to its parent or to one of its children. Return the smallest number of moves after which every node holds exactly one coin.

Trees are written in level order with null for a missing child.

examples.why: The right child's spare coin goes up to the root and then down to the left child. Passing through the root costs a move on each edge.
Three coins leave the leaf (3 moves). Two of them continue past its parent to the root (2 moves), and one goes on down to the right child (1 move).
The only node already has its coin.

constraints: The values add up to n
The tree is at most 500 levels deep
hints: Look at a single edge between a node and its parent. How many coins must cross it, no matter how you plan the moves?
Everything below the edge is a subtree with some number of nodes and some number of coins. The difference has to cross the edge, up if there are too many coins and down if too few.
Post-order DFS: return excess = node.val − 1 + excess(left) + excess(right), and add |excess(left)| + |excess(right)| to the answer.

explain.intuition:
Cut the edge above any node. The subtree below needs exactly as many coins as it has nodes. If it holds c coins and has s nodes, then |c − s| coins must cross that edge, whichever plan you use: surplus has to leave, and a shortage has to be filled from outside. Each crossing is one move, so the answer is at least the sum of |c − s| over all edges.

That lower bound is also reachable: coins never need to cross an edge in both directions, so moving every surplus straight toward the shortage hits it exactly. A post-order walk computes each subtree's excess c − s from its children's excesses, just as a layout pass sums child sizes bottom-up.
steps: For a node, get l = excess(left) and r = excess(right).
Add |l| + |r| to the move count: those coins cross the two child edges.
Return node.val − 1 + l + r to the parent.
Call it on the root and return the move count (the root's own excess is 0).
pitfalls: Counting only coins that move up. A negative excess means coins flow down into the subtree, and those moves count too; take the absolute value.
Summing surplus coins times their distance to the nearest empty node. Shortages compete for the same coins, so local greedy matching goes wrong.
Adding |excess| of the root as well. There is no edge above the root.

solutions.title: Post-order DFS with excess
solutions.idea: Each child edge carries |excess of that subtree| coins. Compute excesses bottom-up and add their absolute values.

solutions.title: Reverse level order, no recursion
solutions.idea: Visit nodes in BFS order, then process that list backwards so every child is finished before its parent. Each node's excess is added to its parent.

followups: The tree is a general tree given as an edge list. What changes?
Each node should end with target[i] coins instead of 1, with the totals still matching. Does the same argument hold?
